This analysis examines the sketch's resilience to corruption in both the data $\boldsymbol{x}$ and the measurement matrix. We demonstrate that to recover a set of $\ell_2$-heavy hitters from $\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{n}$, where $\boldsymbol{n}$ represents $k'$-sparse noise, a corruption-frechet sketch of size $O\big((k + \frac{k'}{ \epsilon^2}) \log (\frac{1}{\epsilon}) \log(m)\big)$ is essential and sufficient. In this formula, $\epsilon$ denotes the heavy hitter threshold (with heavy hitters defined as entries where $v[i]^2 \geq \epsilon^2\|\boldsymbol{x}\|^2_2$) and $m$ is the sketch dimension. Furthermore, we show that the simpler, unrandomized CountSketch fails under general corruptions; however, it achieves optimal, robust performance when data corruption is random, producing an sketch of size $O\big((k + \frac{\sigma_k}{\epsilon^2\mu_3}) \log (\frac{1}{\epsilon}) \log(m)\big)$, where $\mu_3$ is the third moment of the corruption distribution. Numerical experiments validate that our theoretical guarantees closely align with actual performance. Finally, we explore extensions of this result to other structured outliers, self-loops, and the robust recovery of top-$k$ elements. Collectively, these findings underscore the exceptional robustness of CountSketch. Its efficiency and superior robustness properties make it far superior to traditional finite-dimensional matrices like the Hadamard matrix for heavy hitter recovery. This study focuses on HFT strategies known as market making, utilizing the simplest variant called single-sided market making, which involves continuously selling (or buying) at a premium discount relative to the market price. We present a framework called private-strategy. Since HFT practitioners typically lack access to truly private transaction data, we introduce a self-supervised data augmentation approach termed market simulation. We demonstrate that the proposed private-strategy surpasses conventional HFT schemes while still ensuring robust DP guarantees. Notably, our method offers an inherent benchmark for evaluating the effectiveness of existing HFTs. In specific instances, we show that the private-strategy achieves returns superior to non-private HFTs by up to 50%. Furthermore, for every market simulation run, the results prove competitive with standard HFTs. The core contributions of this work are threefold: (1) establishing a systematic and theoretically sound framework for DP in HFT; (2) demonstrating that the private-strategy outperforms non-private HFTs within the DP context; and (3) empirically validating that our method performs as well as or better than non-private HFTs using market simulation. Our empirical findings are based on a comprehensive case study using real-world market data. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first attempt to apply state-of-the-art DP methods to HFT. The source code for the project can be accessed at https://github.com/ChengruiZhu/DpHFT.

We demonstrate that a simple mechanism can achieve a constant approximation of the expected welfare maximization oracle, regardless of the specific distribution or the values of $n$ and $k$. This is accomplished by randomly selecting a single agent and allocating all $k$ items to her to realize the highest possible welfare. Furthermore, our result establishes that an essentially optimal approximation cannot be attained for this class of valuations when only one item is available ($k=1$). Finally, we extend this finding to settings with unknown distributions. Our work complements recent research on first-price auctions with unknown distributions. Designing efficient mechanisms for sum of independent variables models is crucial, as they effectively capture the bounded rationality inherent in real-world agent behaviors. Additionally, our techniques can be applied to achieve constant-factor approximations for submodular functions. Our primary insight involves analyzing agents' expected valuations under random allocation, leveraging the fact that the maximum mean of independent random variables is attained by summing their individual maxima. We demonstrate that agents can be partitioned into two groups, each assigned a portion of the items, such that the resulting mechanism yields nearly the same social welfare as our intuitive baseline. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first proof of constant-factor approximation for submodular functions applicable to continuous, unknown distributions (even bounded ones), representing a more general setting than previous research. we investigated the connection between initial geometric anisotropy and anisotropic flow in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV. Our findings reveal that, outside the very central collision regime, the initial spatial anisotropy shows a strong correlation with elliptic flow across various charged-particle rapidity intervals. Specifically, at mid-rapidity, the anisotropy of the pseudorapidity distribution for charged-pair pairs correlates more closely with elliptic flow than the anisotropy of the mid-rapidity pseudorapidity distribution does. These results support the hypothesis that collective behavior drives the conversion from initial spatial eccentricity to elliptic flow. Additionally, we examined how different participant selection criteria influence initial anisotropy and elliptic flow. Our results indicate that elliptic flow correlates more strongly with the geometric anisotropy of centrality intervals when events are selected based on charged-particle multiplicity compared to events on-shell. This discrepancy may stem from non-central effects in the initial conditions or the varying numbers of participants contributing to centrality determination. Finally, we examined how particle mass affects initial anisotropy and elliptic flow. The observed trends across different particle masses suggest that particle mass influences geometric anisotropy and elliptic flow in varying ways. These results further underscore that the elliptic flow of different particle species originates from the same initial spatial anisotropy. Overall, our findings demonstrate that elliptic flow serves as a direct probe of initial geometric anisotropy. However, we note that the present study cannot definitively isolate the contributions from initial participant configurations to elliptic flow. Future work will explicitly calculate geometric anisotropy for fission events derived from different initial initial-state models. Best linear unbiased predictors (BLUPs) for random effects are fundamental to the analysis of data with specific correlation structures, commonly seen in repeated-measures designs. However, when the correlation parameter is unknown, it is typically estimated concurrently with BLUPs to produce quasi-BLUPs. This paper demonstrates that these quasi-BLUPs remain unbiased if and only if specific symmetries exist within the design's design matrix. Tackling the broader issue of minimizing the squared bias of quasi-BLUPs, we suggest employing BLUPs derived from auxiliary estimates of the correlation parameter, which depend on the data's specific symmetries. Simulations confirm that these new estimators significantly outperform traditional quasi-BLUPs, particularly when sample sizes are small. Furthermore, the method's efficiency in analyzing clustered observational data is highlighted.

While numerous detection methods exist, many rely heavily on handcrafted features and assumptions about both target and anti-spoofing datasets, reducing their effectiveness when applied to new scenarios with limited data. This paper introduces PrPCNet, a lightweight, data-efficient neural network designed to identify live face responses. By leveraging two novel concepts—two-stage learning and self-supervised learning—our model utilizes unsupervised pre-training on attack and genuine images to develop discriminative features. Subsequently, a fully connected layer trained on a limited number of labeled images fine-tunes the model by learning. Handled as a standard classification problem with minimal dataset variation, PrPCNet delivers state-of-the-art accuracy across multiple challenging datasets. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements over fully supervised models trained on small, diverse datasets, proving that our approach outperforms fully supervised baselines even when dataset composition varies. However, its successful application hinges on vast datasets for training deep neural networks. This paper introduces a straightforward yet effective delay-aware data collection strategy designed to generate data-efficient training samples for deep RL agents. We examine two primary approaches for identifying and deferring decisions within environments: an offline method utilizing a straightforward criterion and an online method employing a more sophisticated criterion. Data generated under these delay-aware strategies is then utilized to train agents. We assess performance across three diverse environments featuring varying degrees of uncertainty and infinite state-action spaces. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our proposed methods achieve superior performance with significantly less training data compared to conventional RL techniques. Furthermore, we validate that the delay detection criteria maintain high accuracy in identifying environments with potential for superior performance should decisions be delayed. This framework is versatile, enabling the generic integration of any subsolution-based genetic operator with the probability estimation capabilities of probabilistic queue data structures. Subsequently, we develop and examine two instances of the PQG framework: PQ-EGA and PQ-FGA. In the former, the estimation is based on subsolution probabilities derived using queue adaptive estimates. Our results indicate that while the theoretical bounds prove versatile, prior empirical evaluations of PEA performance were often inadequate due to an over-reliance on a limited set of functions. Nevertheless, both PQ-EGA and PQ-FGA demonstrate superior performance when tested across a population of random functions. Furthermore, among the PQ-guided algorithms, PQ-FGA exhibits robust performance, likely resulting from its ability to estimate the probability of subsolutions with a higher degree of accuracy. Drawing on existing literature, we illustrate that our results extend to a diverse range of algorithms, including queue-based hillclimbing algorithms, standard (non-parallel) evolutionary hillclimbing algorithms, and belief propagation. This confirms that our framework can identify and construct high-performance algorithms across a wide spectrum of techniques grounded in subsolution probability estimation. Consequently, we propose a novel approach for parallel evolutionary algorithm design that promises to deliver robust performance improvements across an extensive array of functions. To enhance efficiency and performance, researchers have increasingly adopted a transfer learning approach where agents are trained on simplified tasks before deploying them to more challenging ones. A notable example is Knowledge Distillation by Hussenot et al., which utilizes an expert model to train a larger agent. Building on this, we introduce a novel method called Curriculum Knowledge Distillation, also inspired by AlphaStar. In this framework, we employ a fixed network, randomly initialized and never trained, to guide a larger agent through a sequence of curricular training tasks. This approach enables scalable learning across numerous environments without requiring the development of any expert models. Aligned with curricular learning practices, we evaluated our method on the harder tasks of Hopper, Pegasus, and Reacher within MuJoCo. Experimental results indicate that our method achieves comparable or superior sample efficiency compared to standard fine-tuning, with our current implementation leaving significant room for further improvement. Our results demonstrate competitiveness against baseline approaches across a variety of environments, both within the known domains (Hopper, Pegasus, Reacher) and on newly introduced environments such as Cartpole-Swingup and MountainCar-Deterministic. While automated segmentation methods are common, they frequently yield sub-optimal results necessitating manual correction, a laborious process that relies on human expertise. This study introduces a "correction-by-planning" system designed for hippocampus segmentation. The process begins with an initial automated segmentation, which typically captures most of the hippocampus but may include errors or gaps. Users then efficiently identify and plan corrections for these local imperfections rather than re-segmenting the entire structure. A key innovation is the integration of free-form deformation (FFD) into a graph-based segmentation framework within a unified time-continuous formulation. In this approach, segmentation is viewed as a time-varying vector field defining voxel positions over a regular grid; automating the actual segmentation becomes simply the automatic planning of voxel motion paths. Consequently, segmentation errors can be corrected by simply adjusting the planned voxel trajectories. We demonstrate that automating hippocampus correction using these methods is both feasible and highly promising. However, we also observed that naive planning approaches often produce non-smooth or unrealistic deformations, highlighting a critical requirement for developing hippocampus segmentation methods that account for anatomical plausibility. Furthermore, we show that incorporating soft-tissue constraints into the objective function can substantially enhance segmentation accuracy. Finally, we present a solution to the challenge of learning appropriate weighting parameters for these constraints from a modest amount of training data. Overall, this work signifies a significant advancement in hippocampus segmentation, paving the way for novel, more robust, and reliable techniques. Additionally, the proposed framework is applicable to other anatomical structures. Experimental results using our method surpass state-of-the-art performance, achieving a mean Dice similarity coefficient of 0.939 (compared to 0.907 for FreeSurfer) and a mean Hausdorff distance of 0.955 mm (compared to 1.373 mm for FreeSurfer). Additionally, we demonstrate that applying our method to improve FreeSurfer's output yields substantial performance gains. The source code will be publicly released. To demonstrate the method's utility, we have also launched an interactive Java applet allowing users to segment hippocampi in 3D T1-weighted MRIs with minimal effort. This paper introduces a three-pipeline training framework grounded in critical expressivity, comprising global model contraction, weight evolution, and link weight rewiring. We propose a pyramidal-like hierarchy—low-mid-high— to guide the global contraction of neural graphs. Furthermore, we introduce a weight evolution process, incorporating an adaptability matrix, to capture varying criticality across different training epochs. Consequently, we design an innovative link rewiring technique, Weight-R, which enhances critical path expression through the innovation matrix. Leveraging the Synergy from these three core components, Weight-R enables the identification of redundant and useful connections through contracted, evolved, and rewritten weight matrices, effectively clearing blockages on critical paths. Synergy is fully demonstrated within the framework, which iteratively applies global contraction, weight evolution, and link weight rewiring to maximize critical path expressivity. This approach facilitates the efficient reorganization of deep neural networks, significantly enhancing both accuracy and inference speed. Extensive experiments on image classification (CNNs) and natural language processing (RNNs) demonstrate that Synergy achieves state-of-the-art inference acceleration without compromising classification accuracy compared to other SOTA sparsification methods. For instance, Synergy reduces ResNet-50 to a 38.1% sparsity level, matching the top accuracy of ResNet-50 (96.3%) while achieving 1.92× faster inference than Pruning and 2.38× faster than Thinning. In contrast, our solution compresses ResNet-101 (95.6% accuracy) to 57.9% sparsity, outperforming all SOTA methods in both accuracy and inference acceleration. For RNNs, Synergy shrinks a ResNet-30 to 59.9% sparsity, achieving 1.61× faster inference than Top-K and 1.47× faster than Random without accuracy loss. Traditionally, the abstract (post-)fixpoint process consists of two stages: an ascending phase that employs widening to ensure termination, followed by a descending phase that utilizes narrowing to refine the result. However, widening often introduces excessive imprecision, resulting in a significant loss of detail during the subsequent narrowing phase. This paper introduces a general framework for calculating (semi-)simultaneous fixpoints to ground post-fixpoint computations. Within this framework, we propose an efficient aborting domain merging strategy. Rather than unconditionally terminating the ascending phase via widening, the algorithm terminates only when merging two successive approximations does not alter the current approximation's values, thereby fully exploiting any residual precision. Furthermore, program analysis can proceed in a hybrid manner by first merging approximations to establish a coarse initial estimate, and subsequently resuming an ascending phase guided by this coarse approximation. Experimental evaluations across a variety of benchmarks demonstrate that SimAbort interpreters enhance both the precision and computational efficiency of ground fixpoint evaluations compared to standard Ascending Widenning Interpretors. The proposed SimAbort scheme can be applied to both Abstract and Over-Approximating interpretations. Over the past few decades, numerous methodologies have been developed to derive analytic approximations for nonlinear systems arising across various scientific and engineering fields [1–20]. This study presents the first observation of Type-C QPOs in SGR 1806-20 during an outburst in 2014. We employed the Cash statistic to identify a significant monochromatic type-C QPO at 28.6 Hz within the hard X-ray to low-energy gamma-ray spectrum (10–100s of keV). Given its high luminosity and the discovery of SGR 1806-20 as a magnetar capable of emitting low-energy gamma rays, we speculate that the type-C QPOs may originate from the Lense-Thirring precession of the magnetar's accretion column rather than the inner accretion disc, a phenomenon previously hypothesized for LMXBs. This finding suggests that the inner regions of accretion columns in magnetars can exhibit QPO characteristics similar to those in LMXBs and provides a novel approach to investigating the type-C QPO phenomenon. We present MatSim, a comprehensive resource consisting of a lexical database of mathematical definitions paired with a concept hierarchy of those same definitions, designed to support both machine and human navigation of large collections of formal knowledge. For machines, MatSim enables the automated generation and reasoning about mathematical definitions via the complete lexicon. For humans, it offers a structured navigation experience through both traditional lexical access and interactive concept hierarchies. This paper introduces our resource, examines the approaches used to construct it, and highlights unusual features and unusual challenges inherent in such large-scale collections. A significant bias, increasing at large scales, is identified in $\xi(r)$, with a notable portion attributed to the subtraction of the second-order Fourier term in the analytic weak limit. This mode coupling bias can be eliminated to any desired accuracy using an expansion in terms of Fourier mode products. A comparable bias exists within $\delta n / \bar{n}$, peaking at scales around $k \sim 0.5 \, h \text{ Mpc}^{-1}$. We demonstrate that this particular bias is also removable through an multipole expansion of the halo density. This formalism enables a clean separation of clustering components. Specifically, it decouples linear halo overdensity modes from nonlinear halo distribution factors; the latter vary with scale due to gravitational dynamics but are universal across different halo mass bins. Applying this expansion to remove clustering factors successfully eliminates the large-scale bias in $\xi(r)$ and the overall bias in $\delta n / \bar{n}$. However, residual scale-dependent bias persists at intermediate scales ($k \sim 0.5 \text{--} 1 \, h \text{ Mpc}^{-1}$), where halo overlap becomes significant. This remaining bias is linked to the non-Gaussian nature of halos within the multipole expansion and is also present in redshift space due to halo pairwise velocities. Finally, we conclude with a comparison of these unbiased estimates against standard smoothing methods applied to $\xi(r)$ and $\delta n / \bar-n$. This alternative approach offers a more efficient approximation of large-scale halo clustering. Ultimately, these findings enhance the comparison between theoretical predictions and numerical simulations, facilitating more accurate cosmological parameter estimation. Additionally, they provide a more reliable method for calculating the angular power spectrum of cosmic shear. In this context, the bias in $\xi(r)$ could significantly impact lensing observables at small scales ($\ell \gtrsim 1000$). Furthermore, we examine the pairwise Kaiser effect at large scales, where it mitigates bias by enhancing clustering. This finding suggests a novel strategy for constraining the Hubble constant using the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation scale in the correlation function. Overall, these methodologies offer a more precise characterization of halo clustering than previously available. Future work will extend this formalism to redshift space

This generalization encompasses the two-dimensional Ising model at its critical temperature, as well as one-dimensional models such as the XY model, eight-vertex model, and a broad class of spin-glass systems. Within the framework of conformal field theory, both the decay exponents in Hilbert space and the temperatures governing the crossover from power-law to non-power-law correlations are directly linked to the central charge $c$ and the Kac table. Furthermore, they imply that only idealized, finely tuned crystalline materials can exhibit true long-range criticality, whereas all interacting solids inherently display an exponential exponential cutoff in their decaying correlations. This conclusion aligns with the physical expectation that interacting systems possess only a finite specific heat at any nonzero temperature. Consequently, alongside the two-dimensional Ising model, our results represent the sole long-standing prediction from physics regarding long-range correlations that remains unconfirmed by short-term or long-term experimental evidence. Consequently, all experimental efforts should now concentrate on verifying or refuting one of our specific conjectures. Finally, our results suggest that the question of long-range correlations should not be abandoned in the search for room-temperature long-range order, but rather shifted to the design and synthesis of novel glassy materials engineered to exhibit ultra-long correlations at accessible temperatures. Elemental abundances were derived via a multi-element, non-local-thermodynamic-equilibrium (NLTE) analysis of one or more key diagnostic lines, designed to mitigate the impact of abundance uncertainties. Line lists were generated using the RADYN radiative hydrodynamic (RH) code to facilitate reliable NLTE corrections. This marks the first application of RADYN-generated line lists for MP/VMP stars. This method was applied to correct 1D photoionization abundances for 25 stars obtained through the YMP project. **Results.** Our analysis reveals variations in abundance patterns among the YMP sample, attributed to the inclusion of all available lines for each element. This work introduces a method to incorporate such errors into secure rate calculations using semi-device-independent quantum information theory. Specifically, we demonstrate that the concept of expected compression can establish a lower bound on the von Neumann entropy affected by systematic errors, which subsequently lowers the lower bound on the length of a secure random string. These techniques enable the calculation of emitter properties—such as eigenenergies, eigenoperators, and correlation functions—from their interactions via virtual excitations within a microwave cavity framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate how these methods can assess the validity of perturbative approximations and how corresponding diagrammatic series can be resummated to extend the range of that approximation. Potential applications include designing quantum networks for emitters that exhibit non-analytical spectral features far beyond the perturbative limit, as well as achieving significant enhancements in emitter correlation functions through constructive interference among multiple virtual processes. Conceptually, these techniques offer a robust theoretical approach for unraveling the complex role of quantum matter-coupled quantum electromagnetic environments in quantum technologies. For instance, in quantum sensing, understanding how coupled emitters respond to external environments is crucial; the proposed diagrammatic method facilitates this by enabling the extraction of effective emitter parameters, including nonlocal couplings to electromagnetic modes. This allows sensors to be tuned to operate at modes that maximize sensitivity while mitigating noise, thereby enabling superconducting quantum sensors to achieve unprecedented dynamical range and frequency resolution. Conceptually, this represents "environment engineering without chemicals," utilizing photons instead. Additionally, a similar approach could extend to phonon engineering in mechanical quantum information systems. As experimental capabilities advance in tailoring quantum environments to optimize various quantum tasks, these techniques will serve as an increasingly valuable design tool. Utilizing an effective model that incorporates spacetime deformation matrices, we analyze how these matrices influence the nucleon's building blocks. Furthermore, we explore the connections between nucleon structure functions and the characteristics of spacetime deformation matrices. Our findings reveal that the behavior of nucleon structure functions varies significantly based on whether the spacetime deformation matrices are symmetric or asymmetric, as well as the magnitude of the noncommutative space-time deformation parameter. Specifically, we observe periodic oscillations when the deformation parameter is small, transitioning to a plateau when it is large; however, asymmetric spacetime deformation results in monotonic changes along specific q² axes. Additionally, increasing the spacetime deformation parameter reduces the contribution of antiquarks to nucleon structure functions. These results offer valuable insights into investigating the microstructure of space-time at the sub-nucleon level. Notably, when spacetime deformation parameters reach the nucleon's energy scale (approximately 1 GeV), the spacetime within a nucleon becomes noncommutative. This suggests potential avenues for researching spacetime properties through nucleon structure functions or for probing spacetime structures at lower energy levels. Given these implications, we anticipate that this work will stimulate further research into spacetime deformation at the nucleon level. Some related findings were previously reported in reference [42]. To facilitate these investigations, we propose that accelerator experiments measuring nucleon structure functions at energy levels between 1 and 100 GeV could serve as a viable tool for spacetime spaceness tests. This study introduces a multiple wavelength imaging instrument capable of simultaneous FUV/Low-EUV observation utilizing plasma-based emission lines. To achieve this, a single, monolithic slit is employed across all channels, and the slit image is directly focused onto thinned CCD detectors equipped with on-chip amplification to handle the low photon flux expected from astronomical sources. This design enables the simultaneous capture of FUV/Low-EUV bands at 121.6 nm (Lyman-$\alpha$), 140.3 nm (CII), and 103.3 nm (OVI) within a compact footprint. This instrument is well-suited for medium-term satellite missions, particularly for solar and H$\alpha$ imaging. It is proposed as a complementary payload for H$\alpha$ astronomy to deliver multi-wavelength imaging data alongside a primary Low-EUV instrument. While recent studies have addressed high-dimensional nonlinear dynamics on graphs with dynamic connectivity, they typically assume perfect knowledge of system parameters. We extend this by tackling distributed optimal control within communication limits where system parameters are highly uncertain. Specifically, this work: 1) develops and analyzes a randomized distributed algorithm featuring uncertain local models and predictive predictions of neighbor states; 2) formalizes the predictive information requirement for local models; 3) establishes sufficient conditions ensuring uniform-in-time recurrence of the closed-loop system; and 4) provides numerical examples demonstrating recovery from arbitrary initial states to steady states with finite average costs. The analysis for 2)–4) is conducted within a nonlinear networked positive linear system framework. Specifically, for positive linear systems, we achieve finite costs, infinite livespan, and arbitrary life span improvements. Building on previous work, the primary contributions of this paper are: 1) the use of local models with predictive information about neighbors; 2) applications within the positive systems framework; and 3) quantitative performance metrics. The methodology in this work is anticipated to be applicable to other distributed control problems. Experimental results confirm that the proposed local control strategy is feasible and effective for achieving distributed optimal control under restricted communication. These findings offer new perspectives on distributed control design regarding communication constraints and robustness to uncertain models. Beyond theoretical advancements, the predictive local modeling approach is expected to be valuable for practical implementations. Although this work focuses on predictive local modeling, alternative strategies such as adaptive local modeling are also promising. The predictive local modeling approach is particularly advantageous due to its simplicity, relying solely on local model identification and communication, which facilitates easier implementation. This paper focuses on the first component, specifically the embedding model, which must capture both content and appearance to detect and retrieve copywrites, including transformative modifications like edits, patches, geometric transformations, and noise. While significant research has addressed image restoration, enhancement, and reconstruction, these areas have not directly influenced the development of content-rich embedding models for write-protection, creating a gap between restoration and embedding detection. We introduce a practical authentication framework based on Bell inequalities, adapted from device-independent quantum key distribution protocols that rely on the Bell loophole-free theorem and the tensor product structure of multi-partite quantum systems. In contrast, our one-way quantization approach relies on the simplex structure. For any $d$-dimensional unital completely positive map $\mathcal{E}$ acting on a $d$-dimensional quantum system, we establish sufficient conditions for authentication under this framework by examining the post-processing behavior of $\math{M}^{\otimes n}$ across $n$ copies of the system, where $M$ is a specific density matrix. Furthermore, we provide a necessary and sufficient condition for a classical randomized sketching technique, known as Johnson-Lindenstrauss (JL) sketching, to achieve authentication. Additionally, we present an efficient protocol for one-way quantization using JL sketching and analyze the post-processing behavior of the JL sketching matrix $\mathbf{A}$. Finally, we fully characterize the post-processing behavior of $\mathbf{A}$, thereby enabling the efficient construction of quantum authentication protocols in uplink multiuser environments. This research offers a comprehensive understanding of the one-way quantization method, with applications extending beyond authentication to tasks such as hypothesis testing, parameter estimation, and the verification of quantum devices. Traditional security methods, such as cryptographic key exchange, face challenges in dynamic IoT environments due to limited resource scalability and node mobility. Consequently, recent research has increasingly adopted information theoretic security, leveraging the physical layer's ability to provide theoretical security guarantees independent of higher-layer assumptions, while aligning with IoT devices' low-power computing capabilities. However, most existing solutions rely on the idealization of perfect secrecy keys, necessitating performance evaluation through simulation rather than direct measurement. This paper introduces an ideal key generation scheme and proposes a straightforward, practical security evaluation method for typical IoT systems. Through numerical analysis, we demonstrate that the security of the ideal key generation scheme can be effectively assessed by measuring the mutual information between parallel received signals. This approach requires the receiver to estimate only first and second-order statistics, significantly simplifying the estimation burden compared to previous methods. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of imprecision in estimating the channel correlation matrix. By applying this security evaluation methodology, we numerically quantify the security performance of an orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) based key generation system. Our results indicate that the security of extracted random keys remains robust even when channel correlation matrices are imperfectly estimated. Additionally, when applied to OFDM-based systems, the proposed security evaluation proves more realistic than simulations based on the assumption of perfect channel conditions. This enables a more accurate estimation of the maximum noise variance under which perfect secrecy can be achieved, thereby facilitating the practical deployment of channel secret key generation systems. Our analysis, grounded in the Ginzburg-Landau framework and under high magnetic fields, attributes this transition to the destabilization of nearest-neighbor vortices by remote-neighbor vortices via the electric field generated by circulating screening currents around immediate neighbors. This mechanism signifies a shift from linear to exponentially decaying screening fields within the vortex lattice and offers a fresh perspective on the lattice's elastic properties. Additional theoretical insights into this phenomenon are drawn from numerical simulations of the Ginzburg-Landau free energy and electromagnetic field equations. This study represents the first observation of a transition marked by exponential changes in sound velocity and compression within a type-II superconductor's vortex lattice. Consequently, it opens a new avenue for investigating electromagnetic field distributions and the vortex lattice structure in high-temperature superconductors using sound velocity measurements within high magnetic fields. Additionally, we propose that this transition may arise from spatially inhomogeneous electromagnetic fields linked to electromagnetic fluctuations near the critical temperature $T_c$ in this class of high-$T_c$ superconductors. Finally, we speculate that this transition may be connected to the enigmatic suppression of $T_c$ by high magnetic fields in high-$T_c$ superconductors. This connection stems from the reduced $T_c$ caused by the electric field effects on the electromagnetic free energy near the transition within the vortex lattice at high magnetic fields and low temperatures. Consequently, these effects offer fresh perspectives on the magnetic field-induced suppression of $T_c$ and the physical origin of such suppression in high-$T_c$ superconductors. We anticipate that measurements of sound velocity and attenuation at high magnetic fields and low temperatures will serve as effective tools for exploring the electromagnetic fields within vortex lattices and the origin of high-field $T_c$ suppression in high-$T_c$ superconductors. Furthermore, we suggest that the electric field effects near vortices at high magnetic fields and low temperatures within the vortex lattice may offer valuable insights into understanding the physics of high-field magnetic field penetration near $T_c$ in high-$T_c$ superconductors. While conventional Raman scattering follows a first-order process, this study introduces a novel second-order scattering mechanism involving both emitted and absorbed excitations with comparable energies. Specifically, when a two-photon input operates under near-resonant conditions with the material, excitations generate a new Raman signal featuring simultaneous multi-photon emission and absorption, termed Resonance-Raman Scattering. Furthermore, we investigate the connections and correlations between DCL-RSPMs and R-2D spin models based on the DCL method, with a specific focus on the (2+1)-dimensional Heisenberg antiferromagnet derived from a DCL process and its relationship to a 2D Heisenberg model exhibiting a topologically ordered completely critical phase (CCP). Additionally, we present a general analysis and approach for determining the magnetic orders of these DCL-RSPMs. Within this framework, we propose new regular magnetic structures (RMSs) and a novel Eulerian graph-based theory (EGT) capable of describing all possible RMSs. This theory indicates that RMSs resembling CCPs may exist in both RSCs and R-2D spin models. We demonstrate that this CEG structure within the DCBL model represents an unusual topological spin phase (STP) distinct from the spin liquid phase. However, this process traditionally demands extensive resources, specifically substantial time and financial investments across multiple test phases. Conversely, employing sound statistical methods without leveraging accurate prior information can result in suboptimal decisions due to experimental challenges such as sampling variability and constraints on time and budget. Our research focuses on developing a decision-making framework for online A/B testing that integrates accurate prior knowledge about treatment effects to enhance the efficiency of in-test actions, thereby improving outcomes for end-users. To achieve this, we introduce a novel Bayesian Causal Bandit framework designed to maximize causal rewards while minimizing computational costs. By adapting the UCB1 index to the Bayesian domain and retaining the original exploration-exploitation duality, our method demonstrates superior performance compared to established benchmarks. Finally, we present two real-world applications to validate the practical effectiveness and feasibility of our approach. These applications demonstrate that our algorithm can significantly reduce the time required to reach a final decision while simultaneously delivering improved end-user results. Through extensive simulations and real-world data analysis, we establish that incorporating prior knowledge into Bayesian A/B testing yields statistically significant performance gains over methods that rely solely on post-experimental data. Furthermore, our algorithm exhibits robustness across diverse data distributions and remains resilient to model misspecification when prior knowledge is only moderately accurate. Specifically, we consider self-energies arising from non-standard contributions by muon and $b$ quark pairs, as well as those from four-quark channels involving electron, muon, $u$, and $b$ pairs. Our results indicate that a muon loop contribution is highly constrained, a direct conflict with the anomalous $W$ boson mass measurement. In contrast, both the $b$ quark and four-quark loop contributions are consistent with the latest LHCb data. Furthermore, the $W$ boson mass derived from the $b$ quark loop scenario aligns with the top quark mass observed in the photon energy spectrum at the LHC. Finally, to further test these findings, we examine the angular distribution of leptons from $W$ boson decays using the Tevaton data; the resulting distribution exhibits sensitivity to the $W$ boson mass and confirms the predictions of the SM framework. We compared reconstructed jet $p_{\rm T}$ distributions against generator-level values to evaluate the potential influence on future $M_W$ measurements. This paper introduces QUICKAR, a novel approach that automatically generates beneficial query reformulations by utilizing crowdsourced data from Stack Overflow. The method evaluates the semantic similarity or relevance between terms by examining their question contexts—specifically titles and tags—to determine if a term should be mapped to a more appropriate candidate. For each concept to be located and every candidate search term, multiple similarity scores are computed and aggregated to produce a single relevance metric, which is subsequently compared against a threshold to select the best reformulation. Empirical evaluations using both real-world and synthetic query datasets demonstrate that QUICKAR outperforms several baseline methods, with a synthetic dataset serving as an effective alternative when real-world resources are scarce and a tag-based variant of the approach showing superior performance. Furthermore, experimental results confirm that QUICKAR surpasses previousarXiv:1903.09934v2  [cs.SE] 2 Mar 20193reformulation approaches on both the Android and Java datasets of the ARKitchar dataset. Additionally, comparisons with state-of-the-art query relaxation techniques reveal that QUICKAR is competitive when query concepts are defined through titles, abstracts, or tags, and it outperforms relaxation methods specifically for term refinement using titles. To investigate how speaker age influences this process, we conducted an age-matched disfluency continuation task where listeners altered their responses based on the test talker's age. Our findings indicate that entrainment is not uniform across the group; specifically, younger test talkers elicited greater fluency disfluencies in their listeners compared to older test speakers. These results offer new insights into the nature of age-related changes in conversation. These implications are twofold: first, they suggest that model-based approaches to dialogue management may need to incorporate information about speaker age, and second, they highlight the need for voice-based conversational agent systems to be calibrated according to the age of the human interaction partner.

This approach, however, relies on students accurately interpreting external terminology and accurately self-assessing. Research indicates that students often struggle to understand testing terminology and are unable to evaluate their own work effectively. To address these educational challenges, we developed TEDUT, a trusted agent within the testing curriculum that facilitates learning by offering curated testing exercises, explaining key terminology in context, and providing external feedback. More importantly, TEDUT acts as a companion during the testing exercise itself by supplying ad-hoc explanations for student queries. We empirically evaluated TEDUT alongside a baseline method using an online experiment. The results demonstrate that TEDUT significantly enhances the student learning experience by improving access to explanations of testing-related terminology and the overall quality of testing exercises. This study provides the first empirical evidence that a trusted agent can serve as an effective companion for students undertaking testing activities. To support practitioners aiming to replicate our methodology, we have open-sourced the source code. Our findings also recommend that future educational tool designers incorporate ad-hoc explanation features into external feedback mechanisms. This work represents an initial step toward a new category of trusted agents designed specifically for testing education. Our specific design decisions and their underlying rationales are documented to facilitate knowledge transfer to other educational domains. By integrating Essential Boundary Current (EBC) and Essential Initial Condition (EIC) equations, the system enhances stability for arbitrary 2D and 3D domain geometries while adhering to physical constraints such as mass and momentum conservation. These EBC and EIC equations are derived from the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) framework using Hyper-Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (Hyper-RANS) modeling to facilitate closure. Furthermore, an integral constraint is implemented to guarantee mass conservation. Validation results demonstrate that these domain-informed equations significantly improve prediction accuracy across diverse scenarios, including 2D/3D flow fields in regular and irregular domains, and 2D/3D flow field mapping in irregular domains. Specifically, combining EBC and EIC with integral constraints reduced prediction errors ($L_{\infty}$-norm) by 74.2% and 64.5% for 2D and 3D flow field mapping tasks, respectively, compared to a standard Vanilla Neural Network (VNNIL). The proposed architecture, characterized by its domain geometric independence, modular structure, and scalability, offers a robust foundation for future research into physics-informed machine learning for fluid dynamics. Additionally, the derived EBC and EIC equations hold broad applicability across diverse domain geometries and their associated boundary conditions. This study presents a novel computational framework designed to estimate the H$^-$ contribution across the full spectral range using the MODTRAN radiative transfer code. We have developed various model grids featuring different electron partial pressures and input opacities to assess their impact on estimated H$^-$ contributions and overall spectral output. These grids have been integrated into the Unified Stellar Atmosphere Codes (USBA) package, enabling the calculation of synthetic spectra that incorporate cloud effects, H$^-$ absorption, and the influences of other species. We applied these model grids to simulate the spectra of the brown dwarf 2MASS J2306-0576 and the super-Earth exoplanet Kepler-186f, generating results that include clouds and H$^-$ absorption. Finally, we compared the simulated spectra against observed data for 2MASS J2306-0576 and a planet resembling early Earth. Our findings indicate that including H$^-$ absorption and cloud effects significantly alters estimated effective temperatures and the spectral energy distributions of both substellar objects and planets. Specifically, for 2MASS J2306-0576, the effective temperature decreases without clouds but increases with a thick cloud layer. For a bare-rock Kepler-186f, the effective temperature rises due to cloud absorption and H$^-$ contributions. These results demonstrate the critical necessity of accounting for H$^-$ absorption and cloud physics when modeling substellar objects and exoplanets. Additionally, we provide further validation for utilizing a simplified H$^-$ approach within USBA, contingent upon selecting appropriate electron partial pressures. This methodology could facilitate the creation of pre-computed grids of H$^-$-enhanced opacities, streamlining updates to standard tables. Furthermore, we have established a feedback loop between USBA and MODTRAN, allowing for the efficient recalculation of spectra using the full spectral library. Although this work utilized two specific examples, the methodology is broadly applicable to any spectrum generated by USBA, provided suitable electron partial pressures are determined. We anticipate that this method will enhance the accuracy of spectra produced by USBA. The accompanying Python package enables users to replicate these calculations and explore various scenarios. By leveraging the frameworks of declarative mapping and homeomorphic declarative specifications, we construct a generalized grounding operator applicable to any first-order declarative mapping. When specialized for ASP, this operator yields a sound and (modulo minimal models) complete grounding procedure. The approach is implemented in the system Grasp; the results of this research constitute the foundational technology for Grasp's second generation. Empirically, the performance of this generation closely matches that of ASP-Ground, the prominent grounding system in ASP-Solver. Furthermore, the paper elucidates and extends earlier findings regarding reverse grounding and grounding with abstractions. The findings in this paper constitute the core declarative grounding methodology of Grasp's current generation. This study examines a super-eruptive C-class eruption of a filament on the Sun's disk, observed on July 13, 2019, using the RHESSI and Fermi/GBM instruments. Although the eruption occurred in the quiet region between about 3.5° and 6° heliographic longitude, both EUV and hard X-ray (HXR) bursts were detected with clear diurnal variations in their spectral and temporal characteristics. Beyond the standard three-phase HXR burst (precursor, main pulse, and phase-advanced footpulses), a distinct gamma-ray flare (GRF) burst with two sub-pulses (G1 and G2) appeared in the 150–800 keV range, displaying a rapid rise followed by a slow decay. This GRF burst exhibits diurnal variations in both its spectral and temporal properties. Through the Fe/H ratio, H$\alpha$ imaging, and multi-heliographic tracking, it was determined that the GRF burst is driven by magnetic reconnection within a post-eruptive magnetic loop. We propose that the GRF burst consists of two phases: the G1 sub-burst results from the initial shock-driven electron acceleration, while the G2 sub-burst is caused by the in-situ trapping of high-energy electrons within a magnetic loop. This event highlights the anti-correlated relationship between spectral and temporal properties of solar eruptions, suggesting a potential diurnal variation in the electron injection rate during GRF bursts. Conventional regression techniques fail to effectively capture temporal interdependencies within such high-dimensional datasets. Consequently, multivariate methods have emerged as essential for modeling physiological traits, offering superior performance in prediction and feature selection compared to basic regression models. We begin by proving that standard differential privacy (DP) techniques struggle to guarantee differential privacy when messages are processed through any standard vector function (DVF). To address this, we introduce a novel concept termed vector-privacy, a stricter variant of differential privacy specifically designed for vector-transformed messages. Vector-privacy demands that every individual entry within a neural network parameter update must independently satisfy the conditions of differential privacy. Leveraging this notion, we unify existing global and local differential privacy methods under the same umbrella, distinguishing them solely by whether they operate on messages after global model aggregation or within a local specific data set. Furthermore, we provide a closed-form equation calculating the total number of possible standard vector functions for a given dimension. This equation demonstrates that the search space for such functions grows exponentially with increasing dimensions, highlighting a constraint in designing differentially or vector-private neural network functions. By viewing standard vector and vector-privacy through this lens, we clarify the underlying principles of various existing DP methods and motivate new research directions. We offer a unified classification of existing DP methods based on the DVF definition, enabling researchers to easily identify limitations in prior work. Additionally, we demonstrate how standard vector and DVF serve as fundamental components in the literature, finding applications across a broad spectrum of areas, including the Bayesian learning theory, and motivating future research efforts. We demonstrate that many prevalent standard vector-learnable functions, currently utilized for differentially private neural network training, inherently satisfy the conditions of the novel concept of "no-use." Finally, we offer a unified classification of standard vector and its inverse, providing a unified framework for their construction and investigation. We demonstrate that there exists a unified class of functions capable of ensuring both standard and vector privacy simultaneously. This review examines various hardware and software approaches designed to speed up these calculations, primarily focusing on algorithms suitable for parallel execution across both parallel computers and supercomputers. The accompanying bibliography is one of the most extensive available, encompassing more than 150 references. Special emphasis is placed on methods that enable simulations involving significantly greater masses and higher temperatures than previously achievable. Furthermore, the text explores techniques for performing accurate computations on fast parallel hardware and identifies current frontiers in computational methods and software for executing molecular dynamics simulations at extreme scales. Key topics include approximate and approximate reversible algorithms, as well as strategies for distributing molecular systems and managing extensive communication and coordinate transformation tasks. The discussion is framed within the context of available computational tools and supercomputer architectures, utilizing performance and accuracy data to compare and contrast different approaches. Finally, the review examines how these methodologies and hardware can achieve extreme-scale computational power required for large-scale molecular dynamics simulations. This comprehensive overview is primarily targeted at computational scientists and developers working on accelerated algorithms and supercomputer applications, as well as on parallel computing methodologies. Furthermore, the text is designed to assist computer scientists and engineers in designing and implementing methods for executing molecular dynamics simulations at extreme scales. It begins with a performance analysis of molecular dynamics computations and a survey of accelerated algorithms, followed by a detailed analysis of approximate and approximate reversible techniques for the extreme ultraviolet and soft x-ray wavelength range. The manuscript also addresses the integration of GPUs into accelerated molecular dynamics simulations and concludes with recommendations for future research, including work extending the applicability of current accelerated algorithms. The primary objective is to provide computer and application developers with insights into the upcoming decade of accelerated molecular dynamics simulations. Additionally, the text will serve as a reference for developing high-performance algorithms for extreme-scale molecular dynamics simulations. This study introduces the First Order Update (FOU) method, which rapidly identifies changes in data stream distributions, detects concept drift, and iteratively selects experts to train on current data segments. FOU operates through rapid iterations, utilizing a time-weighted ensemble strategy to dynamically choose experts based on real-time performance rather than historical metrics. Furthermore, a flexible memory mechanism enables the continual training and selection of experts from old, new, or both datasets as needed. Empirical results demonstrate that FOU surpasses state-of-the-art methods such as Hoeffding Adaptive Gradient Descent (HAGD), Adaptive Gradient Descent (AD), and Online Bagging (OBAG) in diverse scenarios, utilizing less than 50% of the data they consume. Object permanence refers to the capacity to track an object's identity across the entire video, even when it moves out of the visible frame or becomes unobservable. While many current deep learning methods for video reasoning excel at processing visual content, they largely depend on dense frame-by-frame annotations, which fail to capture the temporal integrity of objects present in the full video. To overcome this limitation, we introduce DiocoVision, an open benchmark for video reasoning that relies on sparse temporal annotations and features object-centric questions. DiocoVision comprises 1,200 videos gathered from natural scenes, crowdsourced datasets, and synthetic environments, organized into 3,000 reasoning queries. This study investigates the stability of such three-planet systems by simulating 1000 cases involving three Jupiter-mass planets orbiting between 1 and 10 AU around solar-mass stars. Our findings indicate that the presence of a third giant planet reduces the migration timescales compared to two-planet systems. Specifically, a critical semi-major axis ratio of approximately 0.55 emerges; when all planets reside on the same side of this ratio, migration is significantly accelerated. Conversely, when this ratio is not met—implying a more distributed configuration—the migration timescales show minimal reduction. These outcomes suggest that the three-body interaction effectively acts as if a planet were missing, but only if the planets are not clustered closely on one side of the system. Furthermore, this mechanism offers an explanation for observed exoplanet architectures featuring two giant planets separated by less than a 2:1 resonance, paired with a less massive inner planet. Finally, we conclude that the probability of finding a third giant planet is less than 0.1, whereas the likelihood of having at least one inner planet exceeding 3 Earth masses exceeds 0.5. These predictions can be tested using future three-dimensional exoplanet orbital data. In this context, we identify HD 160697 as a prime candidate for verifying our hypothesis. The system's current configuration matches our predicted final state almost perfectly, with three giant planets on the same side of the 2:1 resonance criterion, consistent with our theoretical conclusions. This final state is estimated to be achieved within less than 10 Myr. Consequently, HD 166097 serves as a valuable target for further investigations into multi-planet system formation. By employing multiple specialized expert networks and a gating network to manage knowledge routing, MoE achieves both high performance and substantial computational complexity. This study reinterprets the MoE framework through a control-theory lens. Grounded in the principle of minimum entropy production, we propose an alternative design that replaces the gating network with a path-finding algorithm based on the entropy of expert inputs. This new formulation treats MoE as a non-convex, nonlinear dynamical system, where each training iteration represents a control task. The objective is to configure expert parameters so that, at any given input, system entropy is minimized via proper knowledge routing. We provide a rigorous theoretical proof demonstrating that this proposed MoE framework guarantees at least equal accuracy and efficiency compared to the original version. Experimental results across standard benchmarks confirm these findings, achieving comparable modeling performance with an average computational saving of 27.9%. Ultimately, this theoretical approach offers fresh insights into MoE construction and highlights future research opportunities viewing MoE as a nonlinear dynamic system. Characterized by its multi-expert architecture coupled with a gating network for knowledge routing, MoE allocates input data to experts based on entropy calculated from each expert's activation state. In this work, we propose an alternative MoE framework grounded in control theory and entropy principles. We interpret each MoE iteration as a control problem aimed at entropy minimization through input routing to appropriate experts. This formulation eliminates the need for a gating network, offering a fresh perspective on MoE construction. The proposed framework achieves comparable accuracy with significantly reduced computational costs compared to the traditional MoE approach. Our experimental findings confirm that this control theory-inspired framework yields improved training efficiency and faster inference speeds. effort to enable deep neural networks (DNNs) to acquire new knowledge while retaining memory of prior experiences through trained weights. This requires rethinking standard deep learning architectures to remember multiple experiences, a goal often pursued by optimizing weight updates to capture shared versus distinct features across datasets. However, since adjusting millions of parameters is often impractical, many recent efforts instead aim to increase the capacity to store multiple experiences by manipulating memory structures. In this work, we propose a novel Deep Cascade Memory module designed to store, recall, and fuse multiple experiences, thereby eliminating the need for parameter tuning. We evaluate this approach by training a single deep network on four distinct datasets—MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100—using Deep Cascade Memory, and compare its performance against other memory-based models like ICELL and Hierarchical System 1/2. Our results demonstrate that Deep Cascade Memory either surpasses or rivals these methods on all tasks, significantly outperforming competitors as memory load increases, and does so with minimal adjustments to model parameters. Additionally, we observe that our system exhibits signs of forgetting, suggesting this is likely due to the inherent constraints of the cascade memory architecture. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of cascade memory within deep networks. A key advantage of Deep Cascade Memory over previous memory-based deep networks is its ability to store an unlimited number of experiences without increasing parameters or requiring retraining. Given its promising outcomes, this method offers a robust framework for continuous lifelong learning. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/DeepCascadeMemory/Deep-Cascade-Memory. Deep Cascade Memory is a foundational component of the Deep Cascade learning system, which replicates human-like learning and memory processes by integrating Cascade, Hierarchical, and Synaptic plasticity. This broader system is detailed in our recent publication: https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.01370. Furthermore, the foundational concept of Cascade Memory originates from UJM's 1980 paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.01370.

This study focuses on optimizing the survival rates of attacks launched by such swarms, specifically targeting the destruction of key ground infrastructure like bridges, power substations, and command centers using an area-of-effect (AoE) weapon. To maximize the efficacy of the AoA weapon, drones must achieve optimal positioning within the immediate vicinity of the target, thereby raising the probability of a direct hit. Given that real-world drone operations face significant uncertainties and adversarial threats, this paper proposes the use of a Swarm Intelligence approach, specifically the Mean Field Game (MFPG) framework, for swarm coordination. The proposed MFG framework is designed to enhance the resilience of swarm attacks against realistic countermeasures, such as ground-based integrated air defense systems (IADS) that utilize both kinetic and non-kinetic means to neutralize drones before they reach the AoE weapon's effective range. This methodology demonstrates robustness by maintaining high attack survival rates even under high uncertainty conditions. Numerical simulations were conducted to validate the approach, utilizing a realistic drone model that incorporates the aforementioned countermeasures. The results indicate successful application with significant improvements in attack survival rates compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, MFG computations required only minimal memory resources, confirming their feasibility for deployment in embedded real-time control units. Additionally, MFG-based swarm attacks exhibit high resilience against countermeasures that adapt their response based on prior observations. Finally, the MFG framework enables the generation of collaborative behaviors that are difficult for human operators to construct, demonstrating the potential advantages of swarm approaches over traditional manned systems. In summary, this paper demonstrates successful real-world application, showing that MFG-based swarm attacks outperform existing methods in achieving high survival rates against diverse countermeasures while utilizing less than 1% of onboard computing resources. By combining a compact hand gesture recognition convolutional neural network (CNN) with policy gradients, we demonstrate a simple framework for interacting with robot swarms: users interact by mimicking user-relative hand movements. We applied this approach to a task-assignment scenario, enabling users to allocate robots to targets simply by tracing the corresponding shapes. We evaluated our system across three scenarios: static targets with static users, static targets with dynamic users, and dynamic targets relative to users. Abstract \begin{abstract} This paper presents a novel Human-Swarm Interaction (HSI) technique designed to control decentralized robotic swarms. Utilizing hand gestures, users can direct a swarm of robots to move between target locations by performing gestures relative to the user. Recognizing this gesture relative to the user enables a decentralized gesture recognition system, allowing users to interact with numerous robots without requiring specific gestures. To demonstrate this capability, we implemented two gestures: an away gesture, indicating a target location away from the user, and a near gesture, indicating a target location close to the user. To move the swarm toward these targets, we employ two methods: utilizing robot vision to map the environment for static targets, or user motion to indicate target proximity for dynamic targets. Furthermore, to prevent robot piling, we implement a topology-preserving configuration-controlling constraint for swarms exceeding six robots. We conducted multiple experiments validating the efficacy of this methodology. Additionally, user testing was conducted to compare our method against existing HSI techniques, demonstrating that our method requires minimal user training, performs well with swarms of any size, maintains precision independent of user distance, supports dynamic targets, and facilitates interaction by gesture. \end{abstract} \textbf{Index Terms}-- Human-Swarm Interaction, Gesture Recognition, Topology Containment Control \section{Introduction} Swarms of robots are

The approach begins by converting the cover image from the RGB to the YIQ color model, followed by a discrete cosine transform (DFT) and a binary search-based compression of the yield matrix to generate a low-resolution image. The proposed framework operates on the principle that features subjected to similar contact histories exhibit comparable gray intensity profiles when captured via scanned images. To identify clusters of similar samples, we treat their image profiles as data points in a high-dimensional space and apply the t-SNE dimensionality reduction method. Although t-SNE is traditionally employed for visualizing high-dimensional data in lower dimensions, we leverage its learned representation to construct a comprehensive, unsupervised sample classification. We have validated this fully automated approach using a scanned image-based unsaturated triaxial apparatus to monitor the macroscopic deformation of soil samples during undrained shear. Our findings reveal that sample behavior during this process can be categorized into four distinct groups based on initial conditions, with specific features evolving differently across these groups due to variations in initial saturation. These results offer new insights into the critical need for precise sample preparation. Additionally, we show that sample differentiation provides critical information regarding shear band formation. We demonstrate a universal correlation between these quantities by varying both the temperature and the strength of the interparticle potential. These findings support the entropy-based variant of the Stokes-Einstein-Debye (SED) relation, which predicts a universal overaging phenomenon where both diffusion and relaxation times diverge linearly with the inverse of residual entropy. Our results indicate that this overaging is not merely an equilibrium effect but persists into the metastable region. Furthermore, we explore the undercooling law governing the SED, which has previously been applied to analyze the caging effect. Finally, we compare our findings with existing experimental and simulation data. These comparisons highlight a widespread breakdown of the SED relation across diverse glass-forming systems, suggesting that the simple entropic framework fails to fully capture the complex undercooled liquid and glassy states. Additionally, we show that the classic SED is actually composed of two independent relations, with the entropy term in the diffusion component exhibiting universal behavior. This universality appears to result from a decoupling of dynamics and dynamic heterogeneity in deep undercooled liquids. Consequently, we argue that an extended SED framework offers a more comprehensive explanation for the underaging behavior observed in undercooled liquids and glasses. Our work also clarifies the specific conditions required for the undercooling law of the SED to apply. Overall, these findings provide new insights into existing theories, particularly the free volume theory and kinetic theory. They suggest that residual entropy plays a more fundamental role than previously thought and may serve as a more robust thermodynamic descriptor of undercooled liquids and glasses than the temperature alone. These represent the first quantitative tests of the SED using molecular dynamics simulations. Such a approach is general and applicable to any glass-forming material, making it a valuable tool for investigating the complex behavior of undercooled liquids and glasses. This work presents analytical calculations for tunneling time within the eEhrenfest framework, which models the dynamics of the classical limit of an ensemble of Schrödinger wave packets under an effective non-linear Schrödinger equation. This study addresses the challenge of detecting parasite eggs in fecal samples by enhancing a deep learning model based on a U-Net architecture. We employed extensive pre-training and training on large datasets of annotated fecal images, followed by fine-tuning on smaller, high-quality datasets from each of the four target classes. This strategy yielded significant performance improvements across all categories. The proposed approach was tested on unseen fecal images in real-world scenarios, successfully identifying three out of four parasite classes with an average accuracy of 91%. Furthermore, the model demonstrates robustness against interference from food particles. To our knowledge, this represents a novel and significant advancement over existing state-of-the-art methods for detecting a specific group of intestinal parasites. Finally, we are offering the complete code and a user-friendly web application to support this research. This work has practical implications for public health, as it can facilitate automated screening and diagnosis, thereby reducing the workload of medical professionals and improving patient outcomes. Additionally, it can serve as a foundation for large-scale epidemiological studies and serve as a risk factor for developing other medical conditions. Providing physicians with assistive tools could also lead to more accurate diagnoses and treatments. These applications contribute to advancements in e-health and medical imaging, ultimately improving healthcare quality and efficiency. Additionally, the web application could be integrated into public health programs to provide services to individuals in need. This work examines how the (n, $\gamma$)-reaction influences the cooling of isolated neutron stars and their pulsar subgroups. We determine the nuclear cross-sections for $^{12}$C+$\gamma$ $\rightarrow$ $^{13}$C $(1/2^+)$ + $n$ and $^{16}$O+$\gamma$ $\rightarrow$ $^{17}$O $(1/2^-)$ + $n$ using the continuous-quantum-discrete R-matrix method. The resulting SRC-enhanced cross-sections are several times greater than previous direct reaction estimates at energies relevant to SRC-cooled neutron stars. Consequently, the predicted lifetimes for these light nuclei to reach their ground states are significantly reduced, potentially producing a distinct class of narrow-radius crusts in isolated neutron stars. Furthermore, the pronounced grouping of pulsars by surface temperature is readily explained. Our findings indicate that the inelasticity generated by the nuclear photo-effect due to SRCs is highly significant. While the photo-effect increases the neutron-to-nucleon ratio, it simultaneously reduces the thermal cooling rate, creating a complex and intriguing effect. Ultimately, our results suggest that the photo-effect plays a more critical role in neutron star cooling than previously thought. Finally, we propose various observational tests to verify the existence of these nuclei. Ultimately, determining the crust's radius or the thermal-timelines of narrow crusts would provide crucial constraints on nuclear physics within neutron stars. In a broader perspective, this research may stimulate investigations into the photo-effect at the extreme energies found in these compact astrophysical objects. Furthermore, extending our calculations to heavier nuclei could yield valuable insights into the cooling and evolution of neutron stars under the influence of SRCs. Furthermore, a direct measurement of these nuclei's cross-sections at energies accessible to modern particle accelerators could enable astrophysical applications of nuclear physics experiments, accelerating our understanding of cosmic phenomena. Conversely, measuring these cross-sections using cosmic-ray data could provide valuable constraints on the photo-effect, thereby advancing our comprehension of high-energy nuclear reactions and their potential applications in energy production. Our analysis reveals that the expected rotational density profile, $p(r)$, decays algebraically as $r^{-\alpha}$ for large $r$. Specifically, $\alpha$ equals $1$ when the particles are in the aperiodic overdamped limit (APOL), and approaches $1$ from above as $\lambda \to \infty$ in the period-modulated overdamped limit (PMOL), where $\lambda$ represents the period. The dynamical density profile for these active dipoles is also derived and compared against the APOL and PMOL models. Furthermore, we determine the dynamical structure factor for these active dipole systems. Finally, the long-range correlations inherent in the density profile of active dipoles are discussed. This study demonstrates that an active matter system can exhibit correlations that persist indefinitely across an infinite domain, thereby establishing a direct link between algebraic decay in density profiles and algebraic tails in time-correlation functions—a phenomenon termed persistent time-correlation. Such persistent time-correlations are also observed in a simple system of self-propelled particles with a finite lifetime, such as an active particle that ceases motion after a specific duration $\tau_p$. Consequently, this work identifies a novel class of active matter systems capable of sustaining correlations throughout an unbounded domain. These findings may facilitate the experimental detection of persistent time-correlations within active matter or related systems. Additionally, given that active matter serves as a prototype for investigating critical phenomena, this research may contribute to the broader understanding of criticality. We note, however, that the density correlations in the systems discussed here are distinct from those at critical points in equilibrium systems governed by the OCB model, as evidenced by the distinct dynamic structure factor in the active dipole system. This suggests that active dipole systems do not belong to the same universality class as critical points in classical Ising systems. We anticipate that these results will facilitate the generalization of critical active matter systems to more complex, biologically relevant scenarios. The experimental validation of these predictions will be the subject of our future research. The methodologies employed here are also applicable to modeling the experimental observation of persistent blood flow in human retinal vessels, a phenomenon that cannot be explained by the Bernoulli principle. Employing a Hamiltonian that integrates Landau-level quantization with a correlation-based wave function, the research compares the computed energy spectra and wave functions against those derived from the Laughlin approximation, which neglects quantization effects. The findings reveal that while the rotational spectrum is significantly softer than in the Laughlin framework, the charge-neutral spectrum exhibits increased stiffness. Additionally, both the ground and first excited states are observed to possess mixed character, combining $m=2/3$ and $m=2/5$ features. This theoreti-cal result addresses and resolves the experimental ambiguity regarding the charge-neutral excitations in this regime. Rotational transitions involving mixed states are calculated, and a proposal to observe charge-neutral excitations in a correlated system involving two high-magnetic-flux high-$T_c$ superconductors is suggested. Furthermore, the two-subband approach is shown to effectively model the coupling between two quantum Hall fluids. Finally, the two-band system's rotational spectrum is found to be substantially softer compared to the Laughlin theory results. These rotational effects are anticipated to be observable in multiple experimental setups involving two correlated quantum Hall fluids.
